It would make an incredible video on geographical barriers and connectivity!

No, the Alaska archipelago (the Alexander Archipelago and the surrounding Panhandle region) was not stolen from Canada. It was originally claimed by the Russian Empire and legally sold to the United States in the 1867.The misconception that it was stolen stem from a bitter 1903 legal border dispute.1. The Russian Claim and the 1825 TreatyDuring the 18th and 19th centuries, Russian fur traders established control over the coastal areas and islands of southeastern Alaska. To prevent clashes with British fur traders expanding westward through Canada, Great Britain and Russia signed the Treaty of Saint Petersburg. This treaty officially granted Russia a narrow coastal strip (the Panhandle) and all adjacent islands, establishing a border that was supposed to follow the coastal mountain summits.2. The 1867 Alaska PurchaseIn 1867, Russia sold its entire Alaskan territory to the United States for $7.2 million. Russia explicitly chose not to offer the land to Canada because Canada was a British colony at the time. Russia had just fought Britain in the Crimean War and wanted to ensure the territory did not fall into British hands.3. The 1903 Alaska Boundary DisputeThe border treaty's language was vague. It stated that the border should lie no more than 10 marine leagues (about 50 kilometers) inland from the "ocean coast".When the Klondike Gold Rush exploded in 1897, Canada desperately needed a Pacific port to access its goldfields in the Yukon.
